beats.text: Morning again. The promised invention is waiting on the pavement below your window, wrapped in a blanket that used to be red.
It's tied with string. One corner is patched with a man's necktie.
"You could've brought it through the door," you call.
"The door has opinions."
The door is a door. Do you say so?
"It knows I'm poor," he says.
"Doors don't know things."
"This one's been trained."
He stops with his hand on the string.
"We," he repeats, like he's testing whether the word holds weight.
"It's my window," you say. "I'm entitled to a share of the crime."
He unties the string one knot at a time, the way people do when they've had things taken off them in a hurry before.
The blanket comes away.
It's a frame. Slats and spars, longer than he is tall, curved at both ends like something's been holding its breath inside it.
Every joint is wrapped in cloth. Copper wire binds two of the slats. The rest are held by nails of every size he could find.
"How many times have you built it?" you ask.
"This version?"
"The question."
He squints at the frame. "Fourteen, perhaps."
Fourteen. Perhaps.

options.label: "Perhaps? You've lost count of your own disasters?"

beats.text: "I stopped counting after the first one broke my nose."
"Which one was that?"
"The third. The first two didn't get far enough off the ground to be rude about it."

options.label: "Fourteen. And you're still out here at dawn."

beats.text: He shrugs, which is a thing he does instead of saying yes.
"The fourteenth one taught me something the thirteenth didn't," he says.
"And the fifteenth?"
"Hasn't spoken to me yet."
"You should keep a notebook," you say.
"I have one."
He says it too quickly, then puts his hand flat against his coat, over the inside pocket, as if the notebook might make a run for it.
He's waiting to see whether you'll ask.
He looks at the window. Then at the notebook. Then at the window again.
He climbs three rungs of the drainpipe and holds it up, open, so you can see without touching.
Oil-stained cover. Pages of figures. Curved spars. Lines of force drawn with a straight edge that was probably a butter knife.
One page is a bird, drawn from below. Every feather marked.
"You drew that?"
"The bird didn't volunteer."
He shuts it before you get to the next page. But he let you have that one.
The silence goes on long enough to become a decision.
He takes the notebook out himself.
"You didn't ask," he says, holding it up toward your sill.
"You'd have said no."
"Yes," he agrees, and opens it anyway.
Curved spars. Lines of force. A bird drawn from below with every feather marked, in a hand steadier than any other part of him.
"Nobody owns the sky," he says, tapping the page. "That's the whole argument."
The kitchen door bangs at the far end of the alley.
The landlord's son comes out with a broom. Seventeen, broad, and fond of finding reasons to use his size.
He sees the frame. He kicks one of the slats.
"Move your rubbish."
Oliver catches the frame before it goes over. "It isn't rubbish."
"Everything you own is rubbish."
The broom comes up. Oliver goes very still, and you understand all at once that he has been hit before and has learned not to move first.
Your hand is already on the window latch.
The boy looks up. Finds a girl in a chair at a first-floor window.
He laughs. "You paying for the pavement?"
"No. I'm paying to watch you make a fool of yourself. Do it without damaging the frame."
He works out slowly that there's no version of the next minute where he looks clever.
He mutters something about tongues and windows, and goes.

options.label: "Careful. That's the landlord's drainpipe you're standing on."

beats.text: The boy stops. Looks down at his own boots on the iron bracket.
"So?"
"So when it bends, he'll ask who bent it, and I'll be at this window, as I always am."
You've never threatened anyone before. It turns out to be mostly arithmetic.
He steps off the bracket, calls Oliver a word you won't repeat, and goes.
Oliver waits until the kitchen door shuts. Then he checks every joint, thumb pressing each knot as if listening for a fault beneath the cloth.
"You didn't have to say anything," he tells you.
"I know."
"He might complain about me."
"He complains when the weather changes."
He laughs. His eyes stay on the frame.
You've started noticing when he laughs. After constables pass. When a room goes too quiet. When his stomach makes a sound loud enough to hear through glass.
"Some people," he says, "would call that courage."
"Would they?"
"Courage is when you could run and don't." You tap the arm of the chair. "I'm just sitting here being rude at height."
He doesn't argue. He also doesn't agree, which is worse.

options.label: "It's the only kind I've got left."

beats.text: You didn't plan to say it. It comes out level, which is somehow worse than if it had wobbled.
Oliver doesn't look up at you with that face people make. He keeps his eyes on the knot under his thumb.
"Then it's a good one," he says.
That's all. He goes back to the wire. You breathe again.
"What's it meant to do?" you ask.
His fingers stop.
"It's meant to leave the ground."
The alley seems to shrink around the words. A bucket tips somewhere above you and water threads down the brick.
Leave the ground.
"No."
"A kite, then. A very large, very stupid kite."
"No."
"You're enjoying this."
"I've waited a long time to be asked properly."
He puts the pliers down. That's how you know it's coming.
"A person," he says.
"A person."
"Me. Off the ground. On purpose."
You close the window halfway. Not for the cold. The room has gone suddenly exposed.
"People don't fly."
"I'm aware."
"Birds have wings."
"So will I."
He says it the way a boy tells you he plans to mend a boot. No performance. He hasn't saved the dramatic part for you.
There's only one question left worth asking.
"Above the roofs first."
"And then?"
"Above the clouds."
That one comes out quieter than the others, and you realise he has never said it out loud before. Not to anyone. Not even to the alley.

options.label: "Why does it have to be you?"

beats.text: He thinks about it longer than you expect.
"Because nobody's coming," he says.
"That isn't a reason."
"It's the only one anyone's ever given me for anything."
Then, quieter: "Above the clouds. That's how high. I'd like to see whether it's blue all the way up or whether it stops."
He lifts the frame and carries it toward the abandoned washhouse at the end of the alley. The door has been off its hinges for years.
You take the chair as far as the broken stones allow. The front wheel drops into a gap and the jolt goes straight up your leg, white and immediate.
Oliver turns at once. You raise a hand before he can reach you.
"Don't fuss."
"I wasn't."
"You were thinking about it."
"There's a smoother path round the back," he says. He doesn't offer to push.
The path behind the washhouse runs beside a wall furred with moss.
He goes ahead of you clearing loose bricks out of the ruts with the side of his boot, and never once looks back to check whether you're managing.
Twice the wheel drops into mud. Both times he waits, hands at his sides, until you ask.
You ask once. He lifts. You don't speak about it.
The broken stones take you four minutes and cost you more than you'd admit out loud.
Oliver walks beside you at exactly your pace, talking the entire way about hinges, so that neither of you has to acknowledge what's happening.
When you reach the doorway he says, "The back path is smoother."
"I know."
"Right," he says, and lets it go, which is the kindest thing he's done all week.
Inside, the washhouse smells of wet plaster and rust. Weeds grow through the cracked floor. A patch of sky shows through the high broken window.
He sets the frame beneath a shelf.
The shelf is where he keeps the rest of it. Thin ribs. A bent pulley. A strip of silk. A brass hinge with teeth like a tiny comb.
You reach toward the hinge.
"Careful," he says, faster than he's said anything all morning.
His hand has come halfway out to stop you, and stopped itself.
"Nothing yet."
"It's brass. You don't own brass."
"I own that."
He takes the hinge off the shelf and puts it in his coat pocket, and changes the subject so obviously that it counts as an answer.
You let him have it. You'll remember the hinge for a long time.
"Only dangerous to fingers," he says, too late to be about the hinge.
"Then it's a strange thing to keep on a high shelf."
"Everything I keep is on a high shelf."
He turns the hinge over once, so the little teeth catch the light, and puts it back where it was, facing away from you.
He crouches beside the chair, at eye level, which nobody does.
"I'll make it work," he says.
"You haven't asked whether I think you should."
"I know what you think."
"Do you?"
He looks up at the patch of sky in the broken window. "You think nobody owns it."
Then he puts both hands flat on the frame.

"You're the first person I've told."

You look at the patchwork blanket, the stolen wire, the raw marks on his knuckles. Above him, through the broken window, a gull turns a full circle without moving its wings.

options.label: "Then I believe you. Don't make me regret it."

beats.text: He nods once, hard, like a man taking delivery of something heavy.
"I won't."
"You can't promise that."
"No," he says. "But you can hold me to it, which is nearly the same and much worse for me."
"Probably."
"Don't say it like that."
"How would you like it said?"
"Like something you'd mind."
He goes quiet. Actually quiet, not the performing kind.
"I'll show you the numbers," he says finally. "Every joint. You can tell me where it's wrong."
It isn't a promise to stop. It's the first time he's offered to let anyone check his work.

options.label: "I want to see what's above the clouds."

beats.text: For a second he doesn't answer, and you think you've said the wrong thing to the only person who'd have understood the right one.
"Then I'll go and look," he says, "and come back and tell you."
"That isn't the same."
"No," he says. "It's what I've got."
Neither of you says anything for a while. The gull comes round again.
The light through the broken window moves off the shelf and onto the floor. Somewhere up on the main road a horse is being shouted at.
"I should get you back before they notice the window's open," he says.
"They won't."
"They might."
"Oliver. Nobody notices the window."
He stops in the doorway with the frame's shadow lying across the floor behind him.
"I do," he says.
The last word of the morning is yours.
"I'm at it every day."
"Be at it where I can see."
He grins, and this time you get the whole thing.
He shrugs. "It was already there."
"You cleared it."
"It was in the way," he says, which is not the same as denying it, and walks ahead so he doesn't have to be thanked twice.
That night you lie awake doing arithmetic you have no business doing. Fourteen frames. One boy. No parents, no trade, no coin.
Above the roofs first. Then above the clouds.
You have been at that window for eleven months, and it is the first thing anyone has ever told you first.

guess.text: "You said a proper invention," you remind him. "I guessed a stolen object."
"It's both," he says, from somewhere behind the blanket. "That's what makes it proper."

hope.text: "You said something that flies," you remind him.
There's a pause from behind the blanket.
"I said I'd show you something," he says. "You're the one who guessed the rest."

default.text: "You promised me something," you remind him.
"I did," he says, from somewhere behind the blanket. "I'm about to be held to it."
